cards.title: The GCP Frontier: GCP in 2026
cards.teaser: GCP in 2026 is recognizable — the same compute, networking, storage, and data primitives — but the strategic direction has crystallized: AI woven into every service, genuine multi-cloud interoperability, and infrastructure that reaches from air-gapped on-prem to the public cloud. This chapter is a snapshot, not a forecast.

runs.text: Note: this chapter is a snapshot dated to early 2026. Specific product names and feature states may shift within the refresh window. The underlying engineering problems each product addresses are framed to outlast the version details.
Three structural shifts define GCP's direction by 2026:

items.text: AI as infrastructure, not add-on.

Gemini capabilities are being woven into Cloud Console, BigQuery, Spanner, Security Command Center, and the developer toolchain — not as optional features but as part of the default operator experience.
Multi-cloud as a first-class architecture.

Cross-Cloud Network, GKE Multi-Cloud, and Cloud Storage Anywhere reflect a platform bet that most large enterprises will not consolidate on a single cloud, and that GCP should be a coherent control plane across clouds rather than a walled garden.
Cloud that extends to the edge and on-prem.
Google Distributed Cloud enables fully air-gapped GCP-compatible deployments in regulated, disconnected, or sovereign environments — bringing GCP semantics to places the public cloud cannot reach.

runs.text: None of these shifts retire existing GCP fundamentals. IAM, VPC, GKE, BigQuery, and the resource hierarchy remain the foundation. The frontier is built on top of them.

This chapter follows the frontier-chapter convention: each card names the engineering problem driving adoption, signals whether a pattern is proven or a strategic bet, and notes real adoption signals where they exist.

GCP in 2026 still runs on the same core primitives, but the strategic bets are clear: AI built into every service, genuine multi-cloud reach, and a version of GCP that works in disconnected on-prem environments. This chapter maps what is new and why it exists.

cards.title: Cross-Cloud Network
cards.teaser: Cross-Cloud Network solves the operational nightmare of connecting GCP workloads to AWS and Azure without building and owning the inter-cloud plumbing. Google owns the physical fiber; the customer gets a managed, BGP-based connection between cloud VPCs.

runs.text: The problem Cross-Cloud Network addresses is real and expensive: enterprises running workloads on GCP and AWS (or GCP and Azure) have historically needed to stitch together a mix of VPNs, Cloud Interconnect, Direct Connect, and custom routing logic to get traffic flowing between clouds predictably. Each hop is a point of failure, a latency source, and a configuration surface.
Cross-Cloud Network wraps that complexity in a managed service backed by Google's private global backbone — the same fiber that carries traffic between GCP regions:

items.text: Managed cross-cloud connectivity.
Traffic between GCP VPCs and AWS/Azure VPCs travels over Google's private backbone rather than the public internet. Latency is predictable; the routing path is controlled.
BGP-based routing.
Standard Border Gateway Protocol — compatible with existing network engineering tooling and mental models.
Single pane of glass.
Network topology, health, and metrics are observable through Cloud Network Intelligence Center rather than requiring separate consoles per cloud.
Co-location with GKE Multi-Cloud and Anthos.
Cross-Cloud Network is a natural complement to multi-cloud compute — the network layer for the same architecture GKE Multi-Cloud provides at the compute layer.

runs.text: Adoption signal: enterprise customers with strict latency SLAs between GCP analytics workloads and AWS-hosted application tiers are the primary early adopters. The pattern of running analytics on BigQuery while keeping transaction processing on AWS or Azure is common enough that cross-cloud connectivity is no longer a niche requirement.

Cross-Cloud Network does not eliminate the need for careful network security design. IAM policies on GCP do not propagate to AWS or Azure security groups. Network-level controls at the ingress and egress points of each cloud remain the operator's responsibility.

Cross-Cloud Network lets you connect GCP VPCs to AWS and Azure VPCs over Google's private backbone instead of the public internet. You get predictable latency and managed routing without building the cross-cloud plumbing yourself.

cards.title: Cloud Run Worker Pools
cards.teaser: Cloud Run was designed for request-driven workloads. Worker pools extend it to long-running, queue-draining, and event-processing workloads — without leaving the Cloud Run operational model. The engineering problem: how do you get the simplicity of Cloud Run for work that is not HTTP?

runs.text: Cloud Run services scale on incoming HTTP requests and terminate idle instances after a configurable timeout. This model works well for APIs and webhooks. It does not work for containers that need to run continuously, drain a Pub/Sub queue, process video, or perform batch inference — tasks with no per-request structure.

Before worker pools, teams running these workloads had two options: accept GKE's operational overhead (Deployment, HPA, PodDisruptionBudget) or use Cloud Run Jobs (which run to completion but do not maintain persistent workers). Worker pools fill the gap:

items.text: Long-running containers, Cloud Run billing.
Workers run continuously and scale based on queue depth, CPU utilization, or custom metrics — not per-request invocation counts.
Same operational model.
Container image, IAM, VPC connector, secrets — all configured the same way as Cloud Run services. No Kubernetes manifests.
Native Pub/Sub and Eventarc integration.
Worker pools can be connected directly to a Pub/Sub subscription. Google manages the subscription pull loop and backpressure scaling.
Autoscaling to zero is optional.
Unlike Cloud Run services, worker pools support a minimum instance count greater than zero — important for workloads where cold-start latency is unacceptable.

runs.text: The honest tradeoff: worker pools sacrifice some of Cloud Run's simplicity for persistent-worker semantics. Teams that need fine-grained pod scheduling, custom node pools, or GPU access will still reach for GKE. Worker pools target the large middle ground of queue-driven and background workloads that GKE was overkill for.
Adoption signal: ML inference pipelines and document-processing backends are the most commonly cited worker pool use cases. Both have sustained CPU/GPU workloads with no natural per-request shape.

Cloud Run worker pools let you run long-running container workloads — queue draining, batch processing, background inference — with the same operational simplicity as Cloud Run services, without needing GKE.

cards.title: Spanner Graph
cards.teaser: Spanner Graph adds native graph query semantics to Cloud Spanner — meaning you can run graph traversals over the same data that your relational queries already read, without ETL, a separate graph database, or a synchronization lag. The problem it solves: graph relationships hidden inside relational tables.

runs.text: Graph databases exist because certain questions — "what is the shortest path between these two entities?" or "who are all the friends-of-friends within three hops?" — are expressed naturally in graph terms but are expensive and awkward in relational SQL (recursive CTEs, multiple self-joins). The traditional answer was to maintain a separate graph database (Neo4j, JanusGraph) and ETL data into it.

The ETL approach has well-known costs: synchronization lag, two consistency models to manage, two operational systems to run, and data drift. Spanner Graph removes these costs by embedding graph query support directly in Spanner:

items.text: Graph Property Language (GQL) queries.
Spanner Graph uses GQL — an ISO-standard graph query language — for traversals. Existing Spanner SQL and GSQL can be mixed with GQL in the same transaction.
No separate store.
Nodes and edges are defined as interleaved tables in the same Spanner database. The same data serves relational and graph queries.
Spanner's consistency guarantees carry through.
Graph queries execute with the same strong consistency and global transactions that Spanner SQL provides.
Schema defined with GRAPH DDL.
A
CREATE PROPERTY GRAPH
statement maps existing tables to a graph schema — nodes and edges — without copying data.

runs.text: Primary use cases: fraud detection graphs (is this account linked to known fraudulent accounts within N hops?), supply chain traceability, knowledge graphs, and recommendation systems that need transactional consistency alongside graph traversal. All of these previously required a graph database alongside a relational one.

Spanner Graph is an example of a converged database pattern — one engine, multiple query models over the same data. The same trend is visible in PostgreSQL (with Apache AGE), Oracle (property graphs), and AWS Neptune Analytics. The bet: operational cost of maintaining separate specialized stores outweighs the theoretical performance ceiling of dedicated graph engines.

Spanner Graph lets you run graph traversal queries — things like multi-hop relationship lookups and path finding — directly over your existing Spanner data, without setting up a separate graph database or syncing data into it.

cards.title: Vertex AI Agent Platform
cards.teaser: Vertex AI Agent Platform is Google's answer to the problem of building, orchestrating, and governing multi-agent AI workflows in production. The engineering challenge: a single LLM call is not an application; a reliable chain of agents that produces consistent output is.

runs.text: The shift from single-model inference to agentic workflows — where multiple AI agents collaborate, call tools, delegate to sub-agents, and maintain state across turns — introduces a class of engineering problems that a raw LLM API does not solve: how do you orchestrate agents reliably, audit their actions, control their tool access, and recover from failures in a multi-agent chain?
Vertex AI Agent Platform provides infrastructure for that problem:

items.text: Agent Builder.
A developer console and SDK for defining agents with tools, personas, memory configurations, and grounding sources. Agents are first-class resources with IAM controls.
Multi-agent orchestration.
An orchestrator agent can spawn, call, and receive results from sub-agents. The platform manages the call graph, handles retries, and surfaces failures in a structured trace.
Tool registry and governance.

Tools (function calls, API endpoints, code execution) are registered centrally. Agents are granted access to specific tools via IAM — the same model as granting a service account access to a Cloud Storage bucket.
Evaluation and monitoring.

Agent runs are logged with full traces (inputs, tool calls, outputs, latency). Vertex AI's Eval SDK can run automated quality assessments against agent traces — a requirement for production governance.
Gemini-native.
Built around Gemini models but compatible with other model endpoints. Grounding against Google Search, Vertex AI Search, or customer data stores is a first-class capability.

runs.text: Honest assessment: the agent platform is a genuine advance over assembling LangChain pipelines on bare Compute Engine, but multi-agent orchestration at production quality remains hard. Trace debugging, non-determinism, and cost per workflow run are real operational challenges that the platform reduces but does not eliminate.

Agentic workflows amplify both capability and failure modes. An agent with broad tool access that receives an unexpected input can take a chain of expensive or destructive actions before a safety check fires. Scope tool access narrowly, set explicit maximum action budgets per run, and treat agent audit traces as a first-class operational artifact.

Vertex AI Agent Platform is GCP's infrastructure for building multi-agent AI workflows — where multiple AI agents call tools, delegate to each other, and collaborate to complete a task. It adds IAM-based tool governance, full run tracing, and production monitoring on top of the raw model API.

cards.title: Confidential Computing Expansion
cards.teaser: Confidential Computing started as a VM-level guarantee: encrypt memory at rest and in use with hardware-backed keys. The expansion into GKE, Dataflow, BigQuery, and Vertex AI addresses the more common case — workloads that are not monolithic VMs but distributed, pipeline-driven, containerized compute.

runs.text: Confidential Computing uses hardware-level trusted execution environments (TEEs) — Intel TDX, AMD SEV-SNP — to encrypt memory while code is executing. The guarantee: even a cloud provider operator with physical access to the host cannot read the memory of a confidential workload. This matters for regulated data (healthcare, finance), sensitive AI model weights, and multi-party computation where data owners must process data without exposing it to the compute provider.

The challenge: modern applications are not monolithic VMs. A data pipeline runs on Dataflow workers. An ML training job runs across GKE pods. A SQL query runs across BigQuery slots. Confidential Computing must reach each of these execution environments to be useful for real workloads:

items.text: Confidential GKE Nodes.

Node pools backed by AMD SEV-SNP VMs. Container memory on the node is encrypted at the hardware level. Works with standard Kubernetes manifests — the confidentiality guarantee is in the node pool configuration, not the pod spec.
Confidential Dataflow.
Dataflow pipeline workers run on confidential VMs. Data processed in memory during pipeline execution — including intermediate shuffle state — is encrypted.
BigQuery confidential processing.

BigQuery slot execution in confidential mode encrypts query working memory. Relevant for multi-party analytics scenarios where data from different owners is joined but neither owner should be able to inspect the other's raw data.
Vertex AI Confidential Training.
ML training on confidential compute nodes. Protects model weights and training data from infrastructure-level observation.

runs.text: Honest caveat: Confidential Computing protects against infrastructure-level access. It does not protect against a compromised application, a poorly configured IAM policy, or an attacker with valid credentials. The trust model is precise: the hardware TEE is trusted; everything above it must still be hardened conventionally.

Adoption signal: financial services and healthcare organizations processing regulated data on GCP are the primary adopters. The EU AI Act and US executive orders on AI safety have increased interest in Confidential Computing for AI model training and inference on sensitive data.

Confidential Computing encrypts your workload's memory at the hardware level so even Google cannot read it while it runs. The expansion beyond VMs means GKE pods, Dataflow workers, BigQuery slots, and Vertex AI training jobs can now all get this guarantee — not just standalone VMs.

cards.title: Carbon Footprint Reporting
cards.teaser: Cloud Carbon Footprint gives GCP customers per-service, per-region emissions data so they can report Scope 2 and Scope 3 cloud emissions for ESG compliance. The engineering problem: sustainability reporting was previously manual estimation; now it is a data product.

runs.text: Enterprise sustainability teams face a concrete compliance requirement: they must report greenhouse gas emissions to regulators, investors, and customers under frameworks like the GHG Protocol, CDP, and the SEC climate disclosure rules. Cloud compute represents a growing share of corporate Scope 2 (purchased electricity) and Scope 3 (value chain) emissions — but quantifying it has historically required manual estimation or third-party tools with indirect data.
GCP's Carbon Footprint product addresses this directly:

items.text: Per-service emissions breakdown.

Emissions reported at the level of individual GCP services (Compute Engine, BigQuery, GKE) and broken down by project and billing account. Useful for identifying which workloads are highest-emissions and prioritizing optimization.
Gross vs. net carbon.

Google reports both gross carbon (before renewable energy matching) and net carbon (after). Google's data centers run on matched renewable energy; net carbon can be zero in many regions. Gross figures are needed for some reporting frameworks that do not accept renewable matching.
Carbon-free energy percentage.
Each region's hourly carbon-free energy (CFE%) is reported — the percentage of time that GCP workloads in that region were powered by carbon-free energy. CFE% varies significantly by region and hour.
Exportable to BigQuery.
Carbon data can be exported to BigQuery for custom analysis, joining with cost data, or integration into sustainability dashboards.

runs.text: The carbon-aware computing pattern that Carbon Footprint enables: scheduling batch workloads in regions and time windows with higher CFE% to reduce emissions without changing the application. GCP's Carbon-Intelligent Computing Service can do this automatically for batch Compute Engine workloads.

Carbon Footprint data is also exposed via the Cloud Billing API, making it accessible to FinOps tools that already consume billing data. Sustainability and cost optimization are increasingly co-managed by the same engineering teams — the data model supports this.

GCP Carbon Footprint gives you actual per-service emissions data for your cloud usage, broken down by project and region. Instead of estimating your cloud emissions for ESG reports, you read them out of a GCP data product — and can shift workloads to lower-carbon regions and time windows.

cards.title: Active Assist Evolution
cards.teaser: Active Assist started as a set of cost recommendations ("you have idle VMs"). It has expanded into an AI-driven recommendation surface across IAM, networking, security, reliability, and sustainability — covering more services and shifting from reactive findings to proactive risk scoring.

runs.text: The engineering problem Active Assist addresses has not changed: cloud configurations drift from best practice over time. Resources are provisioned and never rightsized. IAM permissions are granted and never revoked. Firewall rules accumulate. The question is how much of this drift can be detected and flagged automatically, without requiring manual audits.
Active Assist in 2026 covers a materially broader surface than its original cost focus:

items.text: IAM Recommender.

Identifies service accounts and principals with permissions they have not used in the past 90 days. Recommends role downgrades that preserve actual access patterns while removing excess permissions. Broadly adopted and highly reliable — the recommendation engine is trained on actual usage telemetry, not just policy analysis.
Firewall Insights.
Identifies firewall rules that have had zero matches over a configurable window, overly permissive ingress rules, and redundant allow rules shadowed by more specific denies.
VM Rightsizing.

Analyzes Compute Engine CPU and memory utilization and recommends machine type changes. Now integrated with committed use discount analysis — a recommendation that also includes the CUD impact is more actionable.
Reliability Recommendations.
Flags single-zone GKE clusters, Cloud SQL instances without failover replicas, and Compute Engine managed instance groups below the minimum instance count for availability.
Gemini-powered insight summaries.
In Security Command Center and Active Assist consoles, Gemini provides natural language summaries of finding clusters and risk patterns — reducing the time from alert to understanding.

runs.text: The practical operating model: export recommendations to BigQuery via the Recommender API and build a governance dashboard that tracks recommendation acceptance rate over time. Teams with low acceptance rates for high-priority recommendations are accumulating drift without accountability.

Active Assist is proven for cost and IAM recommendations — these have been in production long enough to have reliable accuracy. Security and reliability recommendations are newer and have higher false-positive rates. Treat recommendation categories differently based on their maturity, and tune suppression rules before automating acceptance.

Active Assist automatically scans your GCP configuration and tells you what has drifted from best practice — excess IAM permissions, unused firewall rules, undersized or oversized VMs, reliability gaps. It has grown from cost-only recommendations to covering IAM, security, networking, and reliability across most major GCP services.

cards.title: Workload Manager
cards.teaser: Workload Manager addresses a gap between capacity planning and deployment: it validates that infrastructure configurations meet the requirements of specific workloads — particularly SAP HANA, SQL Server, and other structured enterprise workloads — before and after deployment.

runs.text: Enterprise lift-and-shift migrations frequently encounter a mismatch problem: the infrastructure that was provisioned for a workload does not actually satisfy that workload's requirements. This is discovered either during testing (expensive but recoverable) or in production (expensive and painful). The root cause is that infrastructure teams and workload teams use different vocabularies — one thinks in VMs and vCPUs, the other thinks in SAPS ratings and memory bandwidth.
Workload Manager closes this gap with workload-aware validation:

items.text: Evaluation framework.

Pre-built evaluation rules for specific workloads (SAP HANA, SQL Server, generic database workloads) that check infrastructure configuration against workload requirements. Rules cover machine type, storage configuration, network topology, and OS settings.
Pre-deployment validation.
Run evaluations against a planned infrastructure configuration before deploying. Catch mismatches before they are provisioned.
Continuous health monitoring.

After deployment, Workload Manager monitors for configuration drift that would put a workload out of compliance with its requirements — storage performance degradation, OS parameter changes, network configuration updates.
Insight integration.
Workload Manager insights surface in Active Assist alongside cost and security recommendations, giving operators a unified recommendation surface.

runs.text: Current adoption: primarily enterprise customers running SAP on GCP. Google has a large investment in the SAP-on-GCP partnership, and Workload Manager's validation rules are most mature for that workload class. The general workload health monitoring capability is newer and less battle-tested for non-SAP workloads.

Workload Manager is a strategic tool rather than a day-one operational primitive. Teams running GKE or Cloud Run workloads do not need it. Teams migrating regulated enterprise workloads to GCP and needing documentation that infrastructure meets vendor-specified requirements will find it valuable.

Workload Manager validates that the infrastructure you have provisioned actually meets the requirements of the workload you are running on it — machine size, storage throughput, network configuration. It catches the mismatch before it hits production and monitors for drift afterward.

cards.title: SaaS Runtime
cards.teaser: SaaS Runtime is a GCP-managed framework for building multi-tenant SaaS applications. The engineering problem it addresses: provisioning, isolating, and managing per-tenant infrastructure in a SaaS product is significant undifferentiated work that most ISVs re-implement from scratch.

runs.text: Independent software vendors (ISVs) building SaaS products on GCP face a structural challenge: every multi-tenant product needs the same plumbing — tenant onboarding, per-tenant resource isolation, per-tenant billing metering, tenant lifecycle management (provision, update, deprovision). This work is not differentiated; it is infrastructure. Yet most ISVs build it themselves, resulting in custom tenant control planes that are expensive to maintain and frequently insecure.
SaaS Runtime provides that plumbing as a managed service:

items.text: Tenant lifecycle API.
Create, update, and delete tenant resources through a structured API. The platform manages the state machine for tenant provisioning, including rollback on partial failures.
Per-tenant GCP project or namespace isolation.
Tenants can be isolated at GCP project granularity (hard isolation, highest cost) or at namespace/VPC-level within a shared project (softer isolation, lower cost). The model is configurable per ISV.
Billing metering integration.
Per-tenant resource consumption is metered and can be used to drive billing through the Google Cloud Marketplace or ISV billing systems.
IAM federation.
End-customer IAM roles scoped to the tenant's resources — customers can manage their own data and users within the boundary SaaS Runtime defines.

runs.text: Honest positioning: SaaS Runtime is early-stage relative to GCP's core services. The pattern it targets is real and the problem is genuine, but the product is more narrowly applicable than broadly applicable. ISVs with complex, differentiated tenant architectures will find it constraining. ISVs building relatively standard multi-tenant SaaS on GCP — database-per-tenant or project-per-tenant — are the target audience.

SaaS Runtime is one component of Google's broader ISV partnership push, alongside Cloud Marketplace and the Partner Advantage program. The commercial context matters: GCP is positioning as the cloud of choice for B2B SaaS builders, and SaaS Runtime reduces the barrier to that commitment.

SaaS Runtime handles the undifferentiated multi-tenancy plumbing — tenant provisioning, per-tenant GCP resource isolation, billing metering, lifecycle management — so ISVs building SaaS on GCP do not have to build their own tenant control plane.

cards.title: Google Distributed Cloud
cards.teaser: Google Distributed Cloud (GDC) brings GCP-compatible infrastructure to air-gapped, on-premises, and sovereign environments where the public cloud cannot reach. The engineering problem: regulated, classified, or data-residency-constrained workloads need cloud operating model semantics without cloud connectivity.

runs.text: A significant segment of enterprise and government workloads cannot run in the public cloud: defense and intelligence systems requiring air-gap; healthcare and financial workloads under data residency regulations that require infrastructure within specific national borders; industrial control systems in physically isolated networks. These customers have been left with two bad options: run on-premises with legacy infrastructure and operating models, or forgo cloud-native tooling entirely.
Google Distributed Cloud closes that gap with two deployment models:

items.text: GDC Connected.

Customer-premises hardware managed by Google, connected to GCP control plane for management. Runs GKE Enterprise, Cloud SQL, and Vertex AI on customer-owned infrastructure. Suitable for data residency requirements where data must stay on-prem but network connectivity to GCP is permitted.
GDC Air-Gapped (GDC Isolated).

Fully self-contained GCP-compatible infrastructure delivered to the customer's facility. No persistent network connection to Google. All management, updates, and software delivery happen through a secure, offline process. Designed for classified environments and networks that may never connect to the public internet.

runs.text: What GDC provides in both models: GKE for container orchestration, a subset of GCP APIs (Pub/Sub, Bigtable, Spanner, Vertex AI for inference), Cloud Console-compatible management UX, and unified IAM. The developer and operator experience is intentionally identical to GCP — the same APIs, CLIs, and tooling work against a GDC cluster.

Adoption signal: GDC Air-Gapped has been deployed in US Department of Defense environments and is the basis of Google's positioning in the US federal classified cloud market. The commercial enterprise version targets European customers with strict GDPR data residency requirements and financial institutions in heavily regulated jurisdictions.

GDC is not a path to running all of GCP on-prem. The supported API surface is a subset of GCP, and not all GCP services are available in GDC deployments. Evaluate the specific GCP services your workloads depend on against the GDC service catalog before committing to this architecture.

Google Distributed Cloud puts GCP-compatible infrastructure in your own data center or a fully air-gapped facility. You get GKE, Vertex AI, Spanner, and a familiar GCP operating model without your data ever leaving your premises — or your network ever touching the public internet.

cards.title: Cloud Storage Anywhere and GKE Multi-Cloud
cards.teaser: Cloud Storage Anywhere extends GCS bucket semantics to multi-region and multi-cloud object storage. GKE Multi-Cloud runs GKE-managed Kubernetes clusters on AWS and Azure. Both reflect the same bet: GCP APIs and control planes should work wherever your workloads run.

runs.text: Two frontier services that share a common strategic root:
Cloud Storage Anywhere

addresses the object storage fragmentation problem in multi-cloud architectures. Each cloud provider has its own object storage API (GCS, S3, Azure Blob Storage). Applications that read or write object storage must handle multiple SDKs, IAM models, and bucket configuration semantics. Cloud Storage Anywhere allows GCS-compatible bucket access to storage that may physically reside in multiple cloud regions — including non-GCP regions. The GCS API is the uniform interface; the underlying placement is managed by the service.

items.text: Single GCS API across regions.
Applications do not change when data placement changes. GCS IAM and audit logging apply uniformly.
Data residency controls.
Bucket-level policies can constrain physical data placement to specific regions while maintaining a globally consistent API endpoint.

runs.text: GKE Multi-Cloud

runs GKE-managed Kubernetes clusters on AWS (via EKS-compatible infrastructure) and Azure (via AKS-compatible infrastructure). The cluster control plane is managed by Google and integrated with GCP IAM. Operators use the same
gcloud
and GKE Console tooling to manage clusters across clouds.

items.text: Unified fleet management.
GKE Enterprise Fleet API treats GCP, AWS, and Azure clusters as peers. Policy, service mesh, and config sync apply uniformly.
GCP IAM for non-GCP clusters.
Cluster authentication uses GCP Workload Identity — operators do not need separate AWS IAM roles or Azure AD service principals for cluster access.
Cross-cloud service mesh.
Anthos Service Mesh connects services running in GKE clusters across clouds with mTLS and unified observability.

runs.text: GKE Multi-Cloud is proven for organizations already committed to GKE Enterprise who need to extend to other clouds. It is not a path to avoiding cloud-specific knowledge — AWS node pools still run on AWS EC2 instance types, and Azure node pools still depend on Azure availability zones. The management plane is unified; the underlying cloud is not abstracted away.

Cloud Storage Anywhere gives you GCS-compatible object storage across multiple cloud regions through a single API. GKE Multi-Cloud lets you run GKE-managed Kubernetes clusters on AWS and Azure, managed from the same GKE console and IAM as your GCP clusters.

cards.title: The Gemini-Native Cloud
cards.teaser: The Gemini-native cloud is not a product — it is a strategic direction: AI woven into every GCP service so deeply that the platform itself becomes an active participant in operations, development, and data analysis. This is GCP's clearest long-term bet.

runs.text: This card is explicitly about a direction, not a delivered product. The engineering assessment below distinguishes what is shipped and proven from what is a stated roadmap intent.

The Gemini-native cloud thesis: every surface of GCP — the Console, CLIs, APIs, and managed services — should have Gemini awareness built in as a default experience, not a bolt-on product. The analogy Google uses internally: the way UNIX shells made command-line tools composable, Gemini should make cloud services AI-composable.
What is shipped and observable today:

items.text: Gemini in Cloud Console.

Natural language queries over your GCP project — "show me all VMs in us-central1 with CPU utilization above 80%" — resolved to Cloud Monitoring queries and rendered in the console. Useful and widely adopted.
Gemini for BigQuery.
SQL generation from natural language, data insights surfaced automatically in the BigQuery Studio interface, and schema documentation generated from column names and sample data.
Gemini Code Assist (formerly Duet AI).
IDE-integrated code completion, generation, and explanation with GCP API awareness. Knows GCP client library patterns and can generate Terraform for GCP resources.
Gemini in Security Command Center.
Summarizes finding clusters, explains attack paths, and suggests remediation steps in natural language — reducing time from alert to triage.
Vertex AI as the model layer for all of the above.
All Gemini-in-GCP features run on Vertex AI, giving customers the same data residency and compliance controls as any other Vertex AI workload.

runs.text: What is a bet, not yet proven at scale:

items.text: Autonomous operations.

The vision of Gemini agents autonomously remediating infrastructure issues, scaling workloads, and responding to incidents is directionally where Google is investing. Production deployments of autonomous cloud operations at significant scale are rare in 2026.
Universal AI-first APIs.
Not every GCP service has Gemini integration at the same depth. Coverage is uneven; the vision of every API being AI-aware is aspirational.

runs.text: The honest strategic read: the Gemini-native cloud direction is credible — Google has the model capability, the infrastructure, and the financial incentive to follow through. The question is execution pace and whether the integrations are genuinely useful or superficially present. Evaluating each Gemini-in-GCP feature on its own merits is more useful than accepting or rejecting the thesis wholesale.

The Gemini-native cloud is GCP's answer to the same competitive question AWS and Azure are answering with their own AI platform investments. All three major clouds are building toward AI-embedded operations. The differentiator will be the depth and reliability of the integrations, not the existence of the strategy.

The Gemini-native cloud means Google is building Gemini AI awareness into every GCP service — Console, BigQuery, Security Center, developer tools — so that the platform itself understands your infrastructure and can help operate it. Some of this is shipped and useful today; some is a roadmap bet. Evaluate each integration on its own merits.
